items.subject: package manager
items.text: The package manager is pnpm 9; do not use npm or yarn in this repo.

items.subject: node version
items.text: Node version is pinned to 20.11 in .nvmrc; run nvm use before installing.

items.subject: monorepo
items.text: The monorepo is orchestrated with Turborepo; pipelines live in turbo.json.

items.subject: env files
items.text: Never commit .env files; only .env.example is tracked.

items.subject: env setup
items.text: For local env, copy .env.example to .env.local and pull secrets from the 1Password vault acme-dev.

items.subject: commits
items.text: Commit messages follow Conventional Commits (feat:, fix:, chore:).

items.subject: pull requests
items.text: Every PR needs one approval from CODEOWNERS and green CI before merge.

items.subject: ci
items.text: CI runs on GitHub Actions; workflows are in .github/workflows/ci.yml.

items.subject: linter
items.text: Linting and formatting use Biome; run pnpm lint at the root.

items.subject: eslint
items.text: Decided to drop ESLint and Prettier in favor of Biome in March.

items.subject: module system
items.text: All packages are ESM: package.json has "type": "module".

items.subject: ERR_REQUIRE_ESM
items.text: ERR_REQUIRE_ESM fix: set "type": "module" in the package and import with the .js extension instead of require().

items.subject: path aliases
items.text: TypeScript path aliases use the @acme/* prefix, defined in tsconfig.base.json.

items.subject: exports
items.text: Prefer named exports; no default exports except Next.js pages.

items.subject: unit tests
items.text: Unit tests use Vitest across all packages.

items.subject: e2e tests
items.text: End-to-end tests use Playwright.

items.subject: coverage
items.text: Coverage threshold is 80% lines; CI fails below it.

items.subject: dependency updates
items.text: Renovate opens dependency update PRs every Monday; automerge only for patch updates.

items.subject: versioning
items.text: Versioning uses Changesets: run pnpm changeset for any user-facing change.

items.subject: answer style
items.text: User prefers concise answers with the code first and the explanation after.

items.subject: lodash
items.text: Avoid lodash; use native array methods or remeda.

items.subject: validation
items.text: Runtime validation uses zod everywhere.

items.subject: dates
items.text: Use date-fns for dates; moment is banned.

items.subject: logging
items.text: Structured logging uses pino.

items.subject: error tracking
items.text: Errors are reported to Sentry; the DSN comes from SENTRY_DSN.

items.subject: feature flags
items.text: Feature flags are managed in GrowthBook.

items.subject: analytics
items.text: Product analytics use PostHog.

items.subject: time zone
items.text: All timestamps are stored in UTC; convert to local time only in the UI.

items.subject: git hooks
items.text: Git hooks run through lefthook; husky was removed.

items.subject: python
items.text: Python scripts in tools/ use Python 3.12 managed by uv.

items.subject: sudo
items.text: Never run pnpm install with sudo; fix permissions instead.

items.subject: ports
items.text: Local ports: web 3000, api 4000, worker metrics 9464, Postgres 5432, Redis 6379.

items.subject: docker
items.text: Local containers run on OrbStack instead of Docker Desktop.

items.subject: local services
items.text: Start Postgres and Redis locally with docker compose up -d db redis.

items.subject: dev server
items.text: pnpm dev at the root starts web, api and worker together via Turborepo.

items.subject: staging
items.text: Staging is at staging.acme.dev and deploys automatically from main.

items.subject: production
items.text: Production deploys happen from git tags v*; the release workflow is release.yml.

items.subject: main branch
items.text: Never force-push to main; it is a protected branch.

items.subject: codeowners
items.text: The platform team owns infra/ and .github/ in CODEOWNERS.

items.subject: comments
items.text: User wants no comments that restate the code; comment only the why.

items.subject: editor
items.text: Recommended VS Code extensions are listed in .vscode/extensions.json.

items.subject: pnpm lockfile
items.text: Gotcha: CI uses pnpm install --frozen-lockfile, so always commit pnpm-lock.yaml after adding a dependency.

items.subject: secrets manager
items.text: Team secrets live in the 1Password vault acme-dev; production secrets are in AWS Secrets Manager.

items.subject: apple silicon
items.text: On Apple Silicon, the sharp and canvas packages need Rosetta-free builds: run pnpm rebuild sharp after switching Node versions.

items.subject: typescript
items.text: TypeScript runs in strict mode with noUncheckedIndexedAccess enabled.

items.subject: issue tracker
items.text: Issues are tracked in Linear under the ACME team; branch names start with the Linear id like acme-123.

items.subject: console.log
items.text: Do not leave console.log in committed code; use the pino logger.

items.subject: license
items.text: The repo is proprietary; the CLI package is MIT licensed.

items.subject: package manager
items.text: The package manager is yarn 1.

items.subject: node version
items.text: Node version is 18 LTS.

items.subject: web framework
items.text: The web app is Next.js 15 with the App Router.

items.subject: auth provider
items.text: The web auth provider is Clerk.

items.subject: auth provider
items.text: The web auth provider is Auth0.

items.subject: auth middleware
items.text: Clerk middleware lives in apps/web/middleware.ts and protects everything except publicRoutes.

items.subject: login page
items.text: The login page is apps/web/app/login/page.tsx and renders Clerk's SignIn component.

items.subject: redirect loop
items.text: Gotcha: the sign-in redirect loop happens when /login is missing from publicRoutes in middleware.ts; also set afterSignInUrl to /dashboard.

items.subject: styling
items.text: Styling is Tailwind CSS v4; config is CSS-first in app/globals.css.

items.subject: ui components
items.text: UI components come from shadcn/ui and live in apps/web/components/ui.

items.subject: server state
items.text: Server state uses TanStack Query; client state uses zustand.

items.subject: redux
items.text: Decided not to use Redux in the web app.

items.subject: forms
items.text: Forms use react-hook-form with zod resolvers.

items.subject: images
items.text: Remote images must be allowed in next.config.ts remotePatterns; the CDN host is cdn.acme.dev.

items.subject: public env vars
items.text: Only env vars prefixed NEXT_PUBLIC_ are exposed to the browser; never put secrets in them.

items.subject: web tests
items.text: Run web unit tests with pnpm --filter web test.

items.subject: web e2e
items.text: Run web end-to-end tests with pnpm --filter web e2e; it needs the dev server on port 3000.

items.subject: storybook
items.text: Storybook runs on port 6006 with pnpm --filter web storybook.

items.subject: hydration mismatch
items.text: Hydration mismatch fix: format dates on the client inside useEffect, or use suppressHydrationWarning on the time element.

items.subject: i18n
items.text: Translations use next-intl; messages are in apps/web/messages/*.json.

items.subject: icons
items.text: Icons come from lucide-react.

items.subject: dark mode
items.text: Dark mode is handled by next-themes with the class strategy.

items.subject: api client
items.text: All browser calls to the API go through apps/web/lib/api.ts, a fetch wrapper that sends credentials: include.

items.subject: analytics provider
items.text: The PostHog provider is mounted in apps/web/app/providers.tsx.

items.subject: can't resolve fs
items.text: Build error "Module not found: Can't resolve 'fs'" fix: add import "server-only" and keep the module out of client components.

items.subject: preview deploys
items.text: The web app deploys on Vercel; every PR gets a preview deployment.

items.subject: caching
items.text: Marketing pages use ISR with revalidate = 60.

items.subject: security headers
items.text: CSP and security headers are set in next.config.ts headers().

items.subject: fonts
items.text: The Inter font is loaded with next/font/google in app/layout.tsx.

items.subject: payments
items.text: Checkout uses Stripe Checkout redirect; the web app never sees card data.

items.subject: accessibility
items.text: Icon-only buttons must have an aria-label.

items.subject: bundle size
items.text: Inspect bundle size with ANALYZE=true pnpm --filter web build.

items.subject: route groups
items.text: Authenticated pages live in the app/(dashboard) route group; public pages in app/(marketing).

items.subject: server actions
items.text: Decided to use server actions for form posts instead of API routes in the web app.

items.subject: error pages
items.text: Global errors are handled in app/global-error.tsx which reports to Sentry.

items.subject: components style
items.text: User prefers small components under 150 lines and colocated tests.

items.subject: web env
items.text: The web app reads the API base URL from NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL.

items.subject: clerk keys
items.text: Gotcha: Clerk dev instance keys start with pk_test_; production builds fail if pk_test_ keys are used.

items.subject: web framework
items.text: The web app is Next.js 13 with the pages router.

items.subject: api framework
items.text: The API is built with Fastify 5.

items.subject: database
items.text: The database is Postgres 16.

items.subject: orm
items.text: The ORM is Drizzle; schema is in apps/api/src/db/schema.ts.

items.subject: db migrations
items.text: Apply migrations with pnpm --filter api db:migrate.

items.subject: generate migration
items.text: Generate a new migration with pnpm --filter api drizzle-kit generate after editing schema.ts.

items.subject: api auth
items.text: The API verifies Clerk session JWTs with @clerk/backend in src/plugins/auth.ts.

items.subject: rate limit
items.text: Rate limit is 100 requests per minute per IP, stored in Redis via @fastify/rate-limit.

items.subject: api versioning
items.text: Routes are versioned under /v1.

items.subject: openapi
items.text: The OpenAPI spec is generated from zod schemas into apps/api/openapi.yaml.

items.subject: api tests
items.text: API tests run against a real Postgres started by Testcontainers.

items.subject: auth tests
items.text: Run only the auth tests with pnpm --filter api test -- auth.

items.subject: stripe webhook
items.text: Gotcha: the Stripe webhook route /v1/webhooks/stripe needs the raw body; register fastify-raw-body or signature verification fails.

items.subject: error format
items.text: Errors are returned as RFC 7807 problem+json.

items.subject: pagination
items.text: List endpoints use cursor pagination, never offset.

items.subject: soft delete
items.text: Rows are soft-deleted with a deleted_at column.

items.subject: money
items.text: Money is stored as integer cents, never floats.

items.subject: ids
items.text: Primary keys are UUID v7.

items.subject: connection pool
items.text: The Postgres pool max is 10 connections per pod.

items.subject: pgbouncer
items.text: Gotcha: PgBouncer runs in transaction mode, so prepared statements must be disabled (prepare: false).

items.subject: database url
items.text: The API reads the database connection string from DATABASE_URL.

items.subject: seed data
items.text: Seed local data with pnpm --filter api db:seed.

items.subject: email
items.text: Transactional email is sent through Resend; templates are React Email in apps/api/emails.

items.subject: jobs
items.text: The API enqueues background jobs to the worker with BullMQ.

items.subject: cors
items.text: CORS allows only origins listed in CORS_ORIGINS.

items.subject: health check
items.text: The health endpoint is GET /healthz and checks Postgres and Redis.

items.subject: request ids
items.text: Every request log carries a requestId header x-request-id.

items.subject: timeouts
items.text: Outbound HTTP calls must set a 10 second timeout.

items.subject: n+1
items.text: Gotcha: the orders list had an N+1 query; use the with: relations option in Drizzle to batch.

items.subject: file uploads
items.text: File uploads go directly to S3 with presigned URLs from POST /v1/uploads.

items.subject: search
items.text: Full-text search uses Postgres tsvector columns, not Elasticsearch.

items.subject: orm choice
items.text: Switched from Prisma to Drizzle in May because of cold-start time.

items.subject: api port
items.text: The API listens on port 4000 locally.

items.subject: migrations
items.text: Never edit a migration that has been merged; add a new one.

items.subject: multi tenancy
items.text: Every table has an org_id column and queries must filter by it.

items.subject: webhooks out
items.text: Outgoing webhooks are signed with HMAC SHA-256 in the X-Acme-Signature header.

items.subject: jwt clock skew
items.text: Gotcha: intermittent 401s came from JWT clock skew; allow 5 seconds of leeway in auth.ts.

items.subject: database
items.text: The database is MySQL 8.

items.subject: api framework
items.text: The API is built with Express 4.

items.subject: cli framework
items.text: The CLI is built with commander.

items.subject: cli bundler
items.text: The CLI is bundled with tsup into dist/index.js.

items.subject: cli package
items.text: The CLI is published to npm as @acme/cli and the binary is named acme.

items.subject: cli config
items.text: The CLI stores its config in ~/.acme/config.json.

items.subject: cli tests
items.text: CLI tests use Vitest snapshot tests of stdout.

items.subject: cli release
items.text: Release the CLI by merging the Changesets version PR; the publish job runs npm publish --provenance.

items.subject: node support
items.text: The CLI must support Node 18 and later; no newer APIs without a fallback.

items.subject: cli esm
items.text: The CLI is ESM-only; the ERR_REQUIRE_ESM error from users means they are on an old Node, tell them to upgrade to 18.

items.subject: cli auth
items.text: acme login uses the OAuth device code flow and stores the token in the OS keychain via keytar.

items.subject: cli local run
items.text: Run the CLI locally with pnpm --filter @acme/cli dev -- <args>.

items.subject: cli colors
items.text: Terminal colors use picocolors, not chalk.

items.subject: cli prompts
items.text: Interactive prompts use @clack/prompts.

items.subject: cli output
items.text: Commands must support --json output for scripting.

items.subject: cli telemetry
items.text: CLI telemetry is opt-out with ACME_TELEMETRY=0.

items.subject: windows paths
items.text: Gotcha: on Windows, config path joins broke; always use path.join and os.homedir().

items.subject: cli update check
items.text: The CLI checks for updates once a day using update-notifier.

items.subject: cli exit codes
items.text: Exit code 2 means usage error, 1 means runtime error.

items.subject: cli link
items.text: To test the CLI globally, run pnpm --filter @acme/cli build then npm link in packages/cli.

items.subject: cli framework
items.text: The CLI is built with yargs.

items.subject: queue
items.text: The worker consumes BullMQ queues on Redis 7.

items.subject: queue names
items.text: Queue names are email, images, billing-sync and webhooks.

items.subject: concurrency
items.text: Worker concurrency is 5 jobs per process.

items.subject: retries
items.text: Jobs retry 3 times with exponential backoff starting at 1 second.

items.subject: scheduled jobs
items.text: Cron jobs are BullMQ repeatable jobs defined in src/schedules.ts.

items.subject: sharp alpine
items.text: Gotcha: sharp fails on the Alpine image; the Dockerfile uses node:20-slim with libvips instead.

items.subject: dead letter
items.text: Failed jobs after the last retry move to the dead-letter queue dlq and alert in Slack #alerts.

items.subject: worker metrics
items.text: The worker exposes Prometheus metrics on port 9464 at /metrics.

items.subject: worker dev
items.text: Run the worker locally with pnpm --filter worker dev; it needs Redis running.

items.subject: job dashboard
items.text: Bull Board is mounted at /admin/queues on the worker, behind basic auth.

items.subject: idempotency
items.text: Every job handler must be idempotent; use the job id as the idempotency key.

items.subject: billing sync
items.text: billing-sync pulls Stripe invoices every 15 minutes.

items.subject: redis memory
items.text: Gotcha: Redis ran out of memory because completed jobs were kept; set removeOnComplete: 1000.

items.subject: worker shutdown
items.text: The worker drains jobs on SIGTERM with a 30 second grace period.

items.subject: image jobs
items.text: Image jobs resize uploads to 3 sizes and write WebP to S3.

items.subject: worker tests
items.text: Run worker tests with pnpm --filter worker test; they use an in-memory Redis mock (ioredis-mock).

items.subject: queue
items.text: The worker consumes RabbitMQ queues.

items.subject: iac
items.text: Infrastructure is Terraform 1.8 in infra/terraform.

items.subject: terraform state
items.text: Terraform state lives in the S3 bucket acme-tfstate with a DynamoDB lock table.

items.subject: cloud region
items.text: AWS region is us-east-1 for everything.

items.subject: kubernetes
items.text: The API and worker run on EKS; the cluster is named acme-prod.

items.subject: helm
items.text: Helm charts live in infra/helm, one chart per service.

items.subject: terraform apply
items.text: Never run terraform apply from a laptop; only the CI plan/apply workflow applies.

items.subject: terraform plan
items.text: Run make plan ENV=staging to see a Terraform plan locally.

items.subject: k8s secrets
items.text: Kubernetes secrets come from AWS Secrets Manager through External Secrets Operator.

items.subject: dns
items.text: DNS is on Cloudflare; the zone is acme.dev.

items.subject: monitoring
items.text: Metrics and logs go to Grafana Cloud; dashboards are in infra/grafana.

items.subject: alerting
items.text: Alerts page the on-call through PagerDuty.

items.subject: kube context
items.text: Switch kubectl context with aws eks update-kubeconfig --name acme-prod --region us-east-1.

items.subject: container registry
items.text: Images are pushed to ECR repositories named acme/<service>.

items.subject: database hosting
items.text: Production Postgres is RDS with Multi-AZ; backups are kept for 14 days.

items.subject: redis hosting
items.text: Production Redis is ElastiCache.

items.subject: eks upgrade
items.text: Gotcha: the EKS 1.29 upgrade broke the ingress; the AWS Load Balancer Controller must be upgraded first.

items.subject: ingress
items.text: Ingress uses the AWS Load Balancer Controller with ACM certificates.

items.subject: infra changes
items.text: Infra changes need a review from the platform team and a plan output pasted in the PR.

items.subject: autoscaling
items.text: The worker scales with KEDA on queue length; the API uses HPA on CPU at 70%.

items.subject: cost
items.text: Cost tags: every resource needs the tags team and env.

items.subject: vpn
items.text: Access to the prod database goes through Tailscale; no public endpoint.

items.subject: rds failover
items.text: RDS failover took 90 seconds in the last game day; the API retries connections for 2 minutes.

items.subject: iac
items.text: Infrastructure is Pulumi in TypeScript.

items.subject: merge policy
items.text: Never merge pull requests yourself; push to the PR branch and let the user merge.

items.subject: pr timing
items.text: Do not open a pull request until the user says the work is ready.

items.subject: branching
items.text: Always work on a feature branch; never commit directly on main.

items.subject: pushing
items.text: Do not push to the upstream remote without asking first.

items.subject: verification
items.text: Before saying a task is done, re-check the work for bugs and security issues.

items.subject: e2e before pr
items.text: Test changes end to end before opening a PR, not only unit tests.

items.subject: explanations
items.text: Explain things plainly, without jargon.

items.subject: research depth
items.text: When asked to research, go deep: read primary sources and cite them.

items.subject: deletion
items.text: Do not delete files or branches without confirmation.

items.subject: friday deploys
items.text: Never deploy to production on Fridays.

items.subject: pr size
items.text: Keep diffs small: one concern per pull request.

items.subject: new dependencies
items.text: Ask before adding a new dependency.

items.subject: generated files
items.text: Never hand-edit generated files under dist/ or *.gen.ts.

items.subject: destructive db
items.text: Do not run destructive database commands (drop, truncate, reset) without asking.

items.subject: full suite
items.text: Run the full test suite, not only the changed tests, before pushing.

items.subject: history rewrite
items.text: Do not rewrite or squash commits that are already pushed.

items.subject: summaries
items.text: End-of-task summaries should be a short bullet list.

items.subject: plan first
items.text: Show a plan before large refactors and wait for approval.

items.subject: git stash
items.text: Do not use git stash; commit work in progress to the branch instead.

items.subject: skipped tests
items.text: Never skip or disable failing tests to make CI green.

items.subject: github cli
items.text: Use the gh CLI for GitHub operations.

items.subject: billing code
items.text: Do not change billing code without the user's review.

items.subject: emojis
items.text: No emojis in code, commits or docs.

items.subject: commit body
items.text: Commit messages use the imperative mood with a short body explaining why.

items.subject: major upgrades
items.text: Do not bump major versions of dependencies without asking.

items.subject: script language
items.text: Prefer TypeScript over JavaScript for new scripts.

items.subject: secrets in logs
items.text: Keep secrets and tokens out of logs and error messages.

items.subject: uncertainty
items.text: When a fix is uncertain, say so instead of guessing.

items.subject: docs updates
items.text: Update the docs/ pages when public behavior changes.

items.subject: ci benchmarks
items.text: Do not run long benchmarks on the shared CI runners.

# Onboarding: acme-platform

Welcome! This page gets you from a fresh laptop to a running stack.

## 1. Tooling

- Install Node via your version manager of choice (fnm or nvm).
- Install Docker Desktop.
- Clone the repo and install dependencies from the root.

### Apple Silicon

On Apple Silicon, the `sharp` and `canvas` packages need Rosetta-free builds. Do not run your terminal under Rosetta.
After switching Node versions, run `pnpm rebuild sharp` or image uploads in the dashboard will crash on startup.

## 2. Local services

See the README for starting the database and cache.

## 3. Checking the stack is up

The API health endpoint is `GET /healthz`. It checks Postgres and Redis and returns 200 only when both respond.

    curl -s localhost:4000/healthz
    {"status":"ok","postgres":"up","redis":"up"}

## 4. Your first PR

Ask your onboarding buddy for a good-first-issue in Linear.

# Ops runbook

## Background jobs

Jobs retry with exponential backoff (5 attempts). Failed jobs after the last retry move to the dead-letter queue `dlq`
and post an alert in Slack #alerts with the job name, payload id and last error.

To replay: inspect the message in `dlq`, fix the cause, then requeue it from the admin UI.

## Database

Production Postgres is RDS with Multi-AZ. Automated backups are kept for 14 days; point-in-time restore is available
within that window. Restores go to a new instance; never restore over the live one.

# Architecture

## Components

- **apps/web**: customer dashboard (Next.js). Talks to the API only; never to the database directly.
- **apps/api**: HTTP API. Owns the database schema and migrations.
- **services/worker**: background jobs. The worker consumes RabbitMQ queues (`invoices.reminders`,
  `webhooks.outbound`, `exports`), one consumer per queue.
- **packages/cli**: the `acme` internal CLI, published to npm.
- **infra**: Terraform for AWS.

### Module not found: Can't resolve 'fs'

A server-only module got imported into a client bundle. Fix: add `import "server-only"` at the top of the module and
keep the module out of client components (move the call into a server component or a route handler).

events.text:
There's a real difference. `structuredClone` copies more types and copies them correctly:
- **Dates** stay `Date` objects. JSON turns them into strings.
- **Map, Set, typed arrays, RegExp, Blob** survive. JSON turns them into `{}` or drops them.
- **Circular references** work. JSON throws.
- **`undefined`, `NaN`, `Infinity`** are kept. JSON drops `undefined` and turns the other two into `null`.

What neither copies: functions, class prototypes (instances come back as plain objects) and DOM nodes. `structuredClone` throws on a function, while JSON silently drops it. On speed, `structuredClone` is usually as fast or faster for large objects. JSON can win on small plain ones, but rarely by enough to matter. Rule of thumb: use `structuredClone` unless you actually want JSON semantics, for example to strip `undefined` before sending a payload.

events.text:
Here's a draft:

> Short version: a 50k export shouldn't starve anything. The CLI pages through the API 200 rows at a time (~250 requests, sequential), so it's one client's worth of load, not a burst. The API scales with HPA on CPU at 70% (3 to 12 pods), and this barely moves CPU. On the worker side, if we later move big exports to a background job, it scales with KEDA on queue length (1 to 20 replicas, a new one per 50 messages), so a big export queue adds workers instead of blocking reminders. The real risk would be one giant DB query, and we avoid that with cursor pagination.

Edit the replica numbers if you'd rather not share them; I took them from `infra/k8s/api/hpa.yaml` and `infra/k8s/worker/scaledobject.yaml`.

```html
<form hx-post="{% url 'hikes:create' %}" hx-target="#hike-list" hx-swap="afterbegin"
      hx-disabled-elt="find button[type='submit']" hx-sync="this:drop">
```
`hx-disabled-elt` disables the Save button while the request is in flight. `hx-sync="this:drop"` drops any second submit that arrives while one is still pending, which also covers pressing Enter twice. For a server-side backstop you could add a unique constraint (user, date, trail) or an idempotency token in the form, but this should stop the duplicates. events.text: side q, is `satisfies` actually worth it over just annotating config objects? lena keeps using it
events.text_all: side q, is `satisfies` actually worth it over just annotating config objects? lena keeps using it

events.text:
Yes, for config objects it's usually the better choice. The difference:
- `const cfg: Config = {...}` checks the object against `Config`, but then **widens** it to `Config`. You lose the literal details: `cfg.routes.home` is just `Route | undefined`, even though you wrote it.
- `const cfg = {...} satisfies Config` checks the same way, but **keeps the inferred type**. Typos and missing keys still error, and `cfg.routes.home` stays known to exist, with its literal values.

It matters most for lookup tables and maps (`Record<string, X>`), where annotating makes every key optional-looking, and for `as const` objects you want validated. Annotate instead when you want the wider type on purpose, e.g. a variable you'll reassign later or a public API surface you don't want to leak details through. Lena's usage is fine.

    acme invoices export --from 2026-08-01 --to 2026-08-18 [--format csv|json] [--out file] [--bom]

- `--format`: `csv` (default) or `json`.
- `--out`: write to a file instead of stdout.
- `--bom`: prefix CSV with a UTF-8 byte order mark so Excel reads accented names correctly.

Retries 502/503/504 responses up to 3 times. Behind the `cli-invoices-export` feature flag.

events.text:
Two things would bite on ElastiCache:

1. `take()` is not atomic: zremrangebyscore → zcard → zadd are separate round trips, so two worker pods can both read `count = limit - 1` and both add. Fix: wrap it in a small Lua script (EVAL works fine on a single-shard cluster-mode-off setup).
2. `reset()` uses `KEYS rl:*`, which blocks the server; ElastiCache lets you run it but it's a bad idea on a shared prod node. Swap for `SCAN` with `MATCH rl:*`.

Nothing else depends on cluster mode. I kicked off three background checks: worker tests, a repo-wide scan for other blocking commands, and a quick local benchmark of the Lua version.

events.text: quick q, structuredClone vs JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) for deep copies — any real difference or is it just style
events.text_all: quick q, structuredClone vs JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) for deep copies — any real difference or is it just style

events.text: Real difference. `structuredClone` keeps `Date`, `Map`, `Set`, `RegExp`, typed arrays, `BigInt` and circular references; the JSON round trip turns Dates into strings, drops `undefined` and functions, turns `NaN`/`Infinity` into `null`, and throws on cycles. Both drop functions and class prototypes (you get plain objects back). structuredClone is usually as fast or faster for anything non-trivial, so prefer it unless you specifically want the JSON normalisation.

events.text:
```tsx
const due = new Date(`${invoice.dueDate}T00:00:00`);
```

Yep, timezone. `dueDate` is a plain calendar date, and `new Date("2026-08-30")` parses date-only strings as UTC midnight, which is Aug 29 evening anywhere west of UTC — so clients in Vancouver (and Toronto) saw the day before. Appending a time makes it parse as local midnight, which is what a due date means.

events.text: random q: 302 vs 303 vs 307, when does it actually matter
events.text_all: random q: 302 vs 303 vs 307, when does it actually matter

events.text: It matters for non-GET requests. **303 See Other** always tells the client to follow with a GET — the right answer after a form POST ("post/redirect/get"). **307 Temporary Redirect** requires the client to repeat the same method and body, so a POST stays a POST. **302 Found** was supposed to behave like 307, but browsers historically switched POST to GET, so in practice it's ambiguous; prefer 303 or 307 to say what you mean. 301 vs 308 is the same split for permanent redirects.

## Local setup

1. Clone the repo and install dependencies from the root.
2. Environment files. Each app has a `.env.example`. For every one of them:
   ```sh
   cp apps/api/.env.example apps/api/.env.local
   cp apps/web/.env.example apps/web/.env.local
   cp services/worker/.env.example services/worker/.env.local
   ```
   Then fill in the secrets from the **1Password vault `acme-dev`** (ask Sam for access).
   `.env.local` is git-ignored; never commit it.
3. Start the databases: `docker compose up -d db redis`.
4. Start everything: `pnpm dev` from the root.

### Billing code

Anything under `apps/api/src/billing/` and `services/worker/src/jobs/billing/` needs Jordan's review before it changes, even small fixes. Open a draft PR and tag Jordan.

events.text: why does next middleware run on the edge runtime by default anyway? feels limiting
events.text_all: why does next middleware run on the edge runtime by default anyway? feels limiting

events.text: Because middleware runs on every matched request before routing, so Next optimised for low latency and global deployment: the edge runtime starts fast (V8 isolates, no Node boot) and can run close to the user on platforms like Vercel. The cost is a restricted API surface — no `fs`, limited Node built-ins, size limits. Recent Next versions let you opt into the Node.js runtime for middleware (`export const config = { runtime: "nodejs" }`), which is worth it if you need Node APIs, at the price of slower cold starts where edge was the alternative.

events.text: ok honest question, useMemo vs useCallback, is there any difference beyond syntax
events.text_all: ok honest question, useMemo vs useCallback, is there any difference beyond syntax

events.text: No real difference: `useCallback(fn, deps)` is exactly `useMemo(() => fn, deps)`. `useMemo` caches the *result* of calling a function; `useCallback` caches the *function itself*. Both only help when something downstream compares by reference — a `memo()`-wrapped child, or another hook's dependency array. With the React Compiler turned on, you mostly don't need either.

events.text: I'd add replicas rather than raise the 5 jobs per process. Reminder jobs are almost all I/O wait (a DB read, the mail call, a DB write), so higher concurrency would help, but every process would then hold more DB connections and mail-provider sockets at once, and a bad batch would fail more jobs at a time. Since the worker already scales on queue length, the cleaner fix is a higher max replica count for the end-of-month spike. If you do want more per process, `WORKER_CONCURRENCY` is read from the environment, so you could try 8 on one deployment first.

Fixed the unused param (it now logs `err: e`).

The stats query had a real bug: it didn't filter by `org_id`, so it summed invoices across every customer. Every table has an `org_id` column, and every query must filter by it (all 27 other route queries do). I added `org_id = ? AND ...` with `req.auth.orgId` as the first parameter. It also lines up with the existing `idx_invoices_org_issued (org_id, issued_at)` index, so the query should get faster too.

Heads up: the infra isn't Pulumi anymore. The Pulumi stack was removed on 2026-08-26 (e40a7b9), and it's now Terraform 1.8 in `infra/terraform` (`required_version = "~> 1.8"`). So the bucket went into `infra/terraform/s3_invoice_exports.tf`, following the existing `uploads` bucket: public access blocked, `local.tags`, and a lifecycle rule expiring objects after 90 days. Nothing is applied; it goes through the CI plan/apply workflow.

The rate limiter is in `apps/api/src/plugins/rate-limit.ts`: `@fastify/rate-limit`, 100 requests per minute keyed by IP, backed by Redis so every replica shares the count, with `/healthz` exempt. I opened issue #1318 with `gh` to track the bucket rollout.

events.text: random q: how is 103 early hints different from http/2 server push? someone said push is dead
events.text_all: random q: how is 103 early hints different from http/2 server push? someone said push is dead

events.text:
Server push let the server send resources (CSS, JS) the browser hadn't asked for yet, on the same connection. In practice it often pushed things already in the browser cache, wasted bandwidth and was hard to tune, so Chrome removed it in 2022 and most CDNs dropped it. So yes, push is effectively dead.

103 Early Hints is an informational response the server sends before the real one, carrying `Link: rel=preload` or `rel=preconnect` headers. The browser decides whether to fetch, and it checks its cache first, so nothing is wasted. It mostly helps when the server needs a few hundred ms to produce the HTML: the browser uses that time to start loading fonts and CSS. Push said "here's the file"; early hints say "you'll probably want this file" and leave the browser in charge.

events.text: while that runs: structuredClone vs JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)), is there any reason to still use the json trick
events.text_all: while that runs: structuredClone vs JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)), is there any reason to still use the json trick

events.text:
Rarely. `structuredClone` handles what the JSON trick breaks: `Date` stays a `Date` (JSON turns it into a string), `Map`/`Set`, typed arrays, `undefined` values, circular references, `NaN`/`Infinity`, and `BigInt`. It's built into Node 17+ and all current browsers.

The JSON trick still makes sense in two cases: when you deliberately want a JSON-safe copy (stripping functions, class prototypes and `undefined`, e.g. before sending something over the wire), or when the object holds things `structuredClone` refuses, like functions or DOM nodes, where it throws `DataCloneError`. Neither keeps class instances' prototypes, so for those you want an explicit copy method anyway.

# ADR 0009: Client state in the web app

Status: Accepted (2026-03-18)

## Context
The invoice editor and filters need shared client state. Options considered: Redux Toolkit, zustand, React context.

## Decision
We decided not to use Redux in the web app. Server state stays in TanStack Query; small client state uses zustand stores colocated with the feature.

## Consequences
- No global store or action boilerplate.
- Devtools: zustand devtools middleware in development only.
- Revisit only if we need time-travel debugging across many features.

The preview failure is a known gotcha: Clerk dev instance keys start with `pk_test_`, and production builds fail if `pk_test_` keys are used. It's under `.github/`, so the platform team needs to approve it.

events.text:
The reviewer's concern doesn't apply: `@acme/shared` is a `workspace:*` dependency of the worker, and `pnpm --filter worker build` succeeds, so the runtime resolves it.

On the CLI: the convention is that exit code 2 means a usage error and 1 means a runtime error (`EXIT_USAGE`/`EXIT_RUNTIME` in `lib/errors.ts`, mapped in `index.ts`). `invoices send` threw plain `Error`s for bad args, so they surfaced as crashes with exit 1. They're now `UsageError`s: a one-line message and exit 2, as the two runs above show. API failures still exit 1. Re-checking it for bugs and security, I also tightened the email check (it used to accept any string containing `@`). The id is validated before it goes into the URL path, so it can't be used for path injection.

Noted for the future: components under 150 lines with colocated tests, and a bug and security pass before I call anything done.

import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto'
import type { Request, Response, NextFunction } from 'express'
import { logger } from '../lib/logger.js'

const HEADER = 'x-request-id'

/**
 * Every request log carries a requestId. It comes from the incoming
 * x-request-id header (set by the web app / ALB) or is generated here,
 * and is echoed back on the response so clients can quote it.
 */
export function requestId(req: Request, res: Response, next: NextFunction) {
  const incoming = req.header(HEADER)
  const id = incoming && incoming.length <= 128 ? incoming : randomUUID()
  req.id = id
  req.log = logger.child({ requestId: id })
  res.setHeader(HEADER, id)
  next()
}

apps/api/src/middleware/request-id.ts
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto'
import type { Request, Response, NextFunction } from 'express'
import { logger } from '../lib/logger.js'

const HEADER = 'x-request-id'

/**
 * Every request log carries a requestId. It comes from the incoming
 * x-request-id header (set by the web app / ALB) or is generated here,
 * and is echoed back on the response so clients can quote it.
 */
export function requestId(req: Request, res: Response, next: NextFunction) {
  const incoming = req.header(HEADER)
  const id = incoming && incoming.length <= 128 ? incoming : randomUUID()
  req.id = id
  req.log = logger.child({ requestId: id })
  res.setHeader(HEADER, id)
  next()
}

events.text:
`AsyncLocalStorage` (from `node:async_hooks`) gives you a value that follows one logical chain of async work. You call `als.run(store, fn)`, and anything `fn` triggers, including awaited promises, timers and callbacks, can call `als.getStore()` and get that same store, without passing it through every function argument. That's why people use it for request context: set it once in middleware, read it deep in a database helper or logger.

On speed: since Node 16 it's built on a cheaper mechanism than the old async hooks, and in current Node versions the overhead is small, typically a few percent in microbenchmarks and usually not noticeable in an I/O-bound API. The real cost is mostly clarity: hidden context is harder to follow than an explicit argument, and it breaks if some library loses the async chain (rare now, but it happens with some old callback-based code).

import { sql } from 'drizzle-orm'
import type { Tx } from '../db/client.js'

/**
 * Next invoice number for an org, e.g. INV-0042.
 * Atomic: the counter row is locked by the upsert, so concurrent creates never share a number.
 * Call inside the same transaction that inserts the invoice.
 */
export async function nextInvoiceNumber(tx: Tx, orgId: string): Promise<string> {
  const rows = await tx.execute<{ n: number }>(sql`
    INSERT INTO invoice_counters (org_id, next) VALUES (${orgId}, 2)
    ON CONFLICT (org_id) DO UPDATE SET next = invoice_counters.next + 1
    RETURNING next - 1 AS n
  `)
  const n = rows[0]?.n ?? 1
  return `INV-${String(n).padStart(4, '0')}`
}

events.text_all: q: does next/image actually proxy remote images through our server? like does every avatar hit our node process

events.text: Yes, by default. A `next/image` with a remote `src` renders an `` pointing at `/_next/image?url=...&w=...&q=...`. The first request for each size makes the Next server fetch the original, resize it, convert it to AVIF/WebP if allowed, and store the result in its on-disk cache (`.next/cache/images`). Later requests for the same URL and width are served from that cache until the cache TTL expires (the larger of `minimumCacheTTL` and the upstream `Cache-Control` max-age). So the first hit per size costs CPU on your Node process; after that it's a file read. Behind a CDN in front of the app, most requests never reach Node at all. If you'd rather skip it entirely, `unoptimized` on the image (or a custom `loader` that points at an image CDN) makes the browser fetch the source directly.

```html
<body hx-headers='{"X-CSRFToken": "{{ csrf_token }}"}'>
```
The token is only in a `<meta>` tag, and nothing sends it. Before, the form presumably had `{% csrf_token %}` inside it; the partial doesn't, so the POST has no token. Putting `hx-headers` on `<body>` makes every htmx request send `X-CSRFToken`, which Django's middleware accepts by default (`CSRF_HEADER_NAME = 'HTTP_X_CSRFTOKEN'`). I made that edit in `base.html`. Side note: `{% load static %}` comes after the first `{% static %}` use there, which will break; move it to the top. Running trailmix's tests in the background.

events.text: unrelated: useMemo vs useCallback, what's the real difference. i always forget when each one matters
events.text_all: unrelated: useMemo vs useCallback, what's the real difference. i always forget when each one matters

events.text:
They're the same mechanism with a different payload. `useMemo(() => compute(), deps)` runs the function and caches its **return value** until a dependency changes. `useCallback(fn, deps)` caches **the function itself**; it's literally `useMemo(() => fn, deps)`.

When it matters:
- `useMemo`: an expensive calculation (sorting or filtering thousands of rows), or an object/array you pass to a memoized child or use as an effect dependency, so it keeps the same identity between renders.
- `useCallback`: a function you pass to a child wrapped in `React.memo`, or a function listed in a `useEffect` dependency array. Without it, a new function each render makes the child re-render or the effect re-run.

If nothing downstream compares identity, both are just overhead. And with the React Compiler enabled, most of this is done for you.

# ADR 0009: ORM

Status: accepted (2026-05-12)

## Context

The API and worker used Prisma. Cold starts on new pods and in the scheduled job runners were 3-4 s,
most of it loading the Prisma query engine binary and generated client. Scale-out during traffic
bursts was slow because new pods took that long to serve.

## Decision

Replace Prisma with Drizzle ORM. Drizzle is a thin TypeScript query builder with no separate engine,
so import cost is small. Schema lives in TypeScript under src/db/schema; migrations are SQL files
generated by drizzle-kit.

## Consequences

- Cold start dropped to ~400 ms in the spike.
- We lose Prisma Studio; use psql or TablePlus.
- Relation loading must be explicit (use `with:`), so watch for N+1 loops.

The workflow runs `pnpm lint`, `typecheck`, `build` and `test` across the whole repo on every PR, and the only cache is the pnpm store, so nothing from earlier runs is reused; the last run took about 14.5 min.

Without changing tools, the standard approach is pnpm's changed-package filter, e.g. `pnpm --filter "...[origin/main]" build` and the same for test/typecheck. That runs only packages changed since main plus their dependents, with `fetch-depth: 0` on checkout so the diff works. For reusing results between runs, we'd need a build cache keyed on inputs, persisted with `actions/cache`. Before I rewrite this: is there already an orchestration layer in the repo that's meant to handle caching? If so, the fix belongs there rather than in raw pnpm filters. I'm pulling step timings for the last 20 runs in the background to see where the 14 minutes go.

```python
Hike.objects.filter(user=request.user).annotate(
    elevation_gain_m=Coalesce(
        Sum("segments__elevation_delta_m", filter=Q(segments__elevation_delta_m__gt=0)), 0
    )
)
```
`Sum` with `filter=Q(...)` becomes `SUM(...) FILTER (WHERE delta > 0)` on Postgres (a `CASE` on SQLite), so only positive deltas count, all in one query. `Coalesce(..., 0)` gives hikes with no uphill segments 0 instead of `None`. # ADR 0014: Move the primary database from MySQL 8 to Postgres 16

Status: Accepted (2026-09-08)
Owner: Marco Bianchi

## Context
We ran MySQL 8 since 2023. Full-text search, JSONB and row-level filtering
all pushed us toward Postgres, and RDS supports it with the same Multi-AZ setup.

## Decision
The database is now Postgres 16. MySQL 8 is retired: the last dump was
imported on 2026-09-07 and the MySQL instance is read-only until it is deleted.

## Consequences
- Drizzle dialect switched to `postgresql` (apps/api/drizzle.config.ts).
- Migrations restart from `0031_pg_baseline.sql`.
- Local dev uses the `postgres:16` image in docker-compose.yml.
- DATABASE_URL format changes to postgres://user:pass@host:5432/acme.

events.text:
```ts
const rounded = Number(`${Math.round(Number(`${amount}e2`))}e-2`)
```
The old code did `Math.round(amount * 100)`, and `2.005 * 100` is `200.49999999999997` in floating point, so it rounded down. Shifting the decimal point through the string form avoids the multiply. Most callers pass cents divided by 100, so the real long-term fix is to format straight from integer cents, but this unblocks Lena's invoice.

node -e "const f=new Intl.NumberFormat('en-CA',{style:'currency',currency:'CAD',roundingMode:'halfEven'});console.log(f.format(2.125),f.resolvedOptions().roundingMode)"

events.text:
Yes. `roundingMode` came in with Intl.NumberFormat v3 (ES2023) and is in every current engine: V8 since Chrome 106 / Node 19.x+, Safari 15.4, Firefox 116. The values are `ceil`, `floor`, `expand`, `trunc`, `halfCeil`, `halfFloor`, `halfExpand` (the default), `halfTrunc` and `halfEven` (banker's rounding). There are also `roundingIncrement` (e.g. round to 0.05 for cash) and `roundingPriority`.

One catch: it rounds the binary double you pass in, so `2.005` is already `2.00499...` before Intl sees it and `halfExpand` still gives 2.00. It doesn't replace the decimal-shift fix; it only controls the tie-breaking rule. Formatting from a string (`format('2.005')`, also allowed in v3) does keep the exact decimal.

The three files are fixed too: `bulk-actions.tsx` now passes `status={k}`, the filter spreads `status: s`, and the stories use `args: { status }`.

`allTextContents()` reads the rows once, right after the click, without waiting. The sort refetches from the server, so on a slow run you read the old unsorted rows. Your received array is exactly the seed order, which confirms it. `toHaveText` with an array retries until the rows match (or times out), and the `aria-sort` check makes sure both clicks landed. 30/30 passed with `--repeat-each=15`.

`python -m venv` copies whichever `python` runs it, so her shell is resolving `python` to the system 3.10, not the pyenv shim. Things to check, in order:

1. `which python` and `pyenv which python` inside the project. If the first isn't `~/.pyenv/shims/python`, pyenv isn't initialised in that shell: she needs `eval "$(pyenv init -)"` in `~/.bashrc` or `~/.zshrc` (not only in `.profile`, which non-login shells skip).
2. `pyenv version` in the project dir. Without a `.python-version` file it falls back to the global, which may be `system`. `pyenv local 3.12.6` writes the file.
3. Then recreate it: `rm -rf .venv && python -m venv .venv`. An existing venv keeps pointing at the interpreter it was made with.

Fastest sanity check: `~/.pyenv/versions/3.12.6/bin/python -m venv .venv` bypasses all of that, and if that works it's definitely the shell init.

events.text:
Yes to both. The CSP and security headers are set in `apps/web/next.config.ts`, in `headers()`, applied to every route (`/:path*`), and production returns them:

- `Content-Security-Policy` with `frame-ancestors 'none'`
- `X-Frame-Options: DENY` (the legacy equivalent, for older browsers)
- HSTS with a 2-year max-age plus preload, `nosniff`, `strict-origin-when-cross-origin` referrer, and a Permissions-Policy that disables camera, mic and geolocation.

One honest caveat for the questionnaire: `script-src` allows `'unsafe-inline'`, so the policy limits where scripts load from but doesn't block inline script injection. Moving to nonces would fix that, and it's a bigger change.

Draft reply:

> Hi, thanks for reporting this and sorry for the trouble. To narrow it down, could you run the tool once more and paste the full message it prints, plus the output of `process.version` (or your runtime's `--version`)? In the meantime, the usual fix is: install the current LTS release of the JavaScript runtime, open a new shell, reinstall the tool globally with your package manager, then run it with `--help` to confirm it starts.

I left the package name and exact install command generic because I'm not sure which name we ship it under; fill those in or tell me and I'll update the draft.

The code: `src/lib/runtime-check.ts` runs before `main.js` is loaded (it's a dynamic import now), so a too-low version prints a yellow warning to stderr and exits 1 instead of crashing. I picked 20 as the floor as a guess; set `MIN_MAJOR` to whatever we actually support. I used plain escape codes for the color; if the CLI already has a color helper I should swap it in. Running the CLI tests in the background.

events.text: q: for cli output meant for jq, is a pretty-printed json array better or json lines? what do other tools do
events.text_all: q: for cli output meant for jq, is a pretty-printed json array better or json lines? what do other tools do

events.text:
For piping, JSON Lines (one compact object per line) is usually the better default once output can get big; a single array is fine for small, bounded output.

- **Array**: `jq` has to read the whole document before it emits anything, and the producer has to finish before the output is valid JSON. Easy for consumers (`jq '.[] | .number'`), and pretty-printing costs nothing for jq.
- **JSON Lines**: streams. Each line is valid on its own, so `head`, `grep`, `wc -l` and `jq -c 'select(.status=="overdue")'` work line by line, and a partial output (Ctrl-C, pagination) is still usable. `jq -s` turns it back into an array when you need one.

What others do: `gh` prints arrays with `--json` (bounded by `--limit`); `kubectl -o json` prints one wrapped object; `docker ... --format '{{json .}}'` and `aws logs` style tools stream one object per line; `jq` itself, `ripgrep --json` and most log tools use JSON Lines.

For `invoices list` with a `--limit`, the array is fine. If you ever add `--all` that pages through everything, add `--jsonl` for that case rather than changing `--json`.

events.text:
```python
template = "hikes/_form.html" if request.headers.get("HX-Request") else "hikes/create.html"
return render(request, template, {"form": form})
```

When htmx posts, it sends an `HX-Request` header, so the view now returns only `_form.html` on validation errors and your `hx-target="this" hx-swap="outerHTML"` replaces just the form. On success it answers 204 with `HX-Redirect` so htmx does a normal navigation to the detail page. Make sure `_form.html` contains the `<form>` tag itself, otherwise you'll get a form nested inside a form after the swap. If you end up doing this in many views, `django-htmx` gives you `request.htmx` instead of reading the header by hand.

`select_related` for trail and region: they're foreign keys, so Django joins them into the same query instead of 2 extra queries per row (that's ~4k queries today for 2k hikes). `prefetch_related` is for the many-to-many tags, which can't be joined; it does one extra query for all of them. # Payments architecture

Last updated: 2026-08-28 (Marco)

## Overview

Agencies get paid by their clients through Acme invoices. We never handle
raw card numbers.

## Checkout

Checkout uses Stripe Checkout in redirect mode. The web app creates a
Checkout Session through the API and redirects the browser to Stripe. The
web app never sees card data; it only receives the session id on the
success URL.

## Webhooks

Stripe calls POST /v1/webhooks/stripe. The API verifies the signature,
stores the event in stripe_events (idempotent on event id), and enqueues
a job to update the invoice status.

## Payouts

When Stripe pays out to an agency's connected account, the payout.paid
webhook creates a row in payouts. Agencies see their payouts in the
dashboard under Settings > Payouts.

## Open questions

- Do we backfill payouts created before the connected-account migration?

# apps/web

The Acme customer dashboard.

## Stack

- Auth: Clerk (we moved off Auth0 in August; see ACME-171). Middleware is in
  middleware.ts.
- Hosting: the web app deploys on Vercel. Every PR gets a preview deployment;
  the link is posted on the PR by the Vercel bot.
- UI: shadcn/ui components in components/ui, Tailwind for styling.
- Data: TanStack Query for server state, zustand for client state.

## Decisions

- Form posts use server actions instead of API routes. We decided this in
  July so validation and redirects live next to the form. Do not add new
  files under app/api/ for form submissions.
- No Redux.

## Getting started

1. `yarn install`
2. `cp .env.example .env.local`
3. `yarn dev` and open http://localhost:3000

## Scripts

| Script | What |
|---|---|
| `yarn test` | unit tests |
| `yarn lint` | ESLint |
| `yarn storybook` | Storybook |

## Folder layout

- pages/ - routes
- components/ - shared components
- lib/ - helpers

events.text:
Both date cells now use next-intl's `useFormatter` (hook added at the top of each component), so server and client format the same way.

On the worker log: yes, worth fixing, though nothing is lost. image-resize jobs take 7.5-9s but that queue's `lockDuration` is 5000 ms, so the lock expires mid-job, the stall checker thinks the worker died and puts the job back in wait. Each one then runs a second time, so every image is resized twice and it will eventually count against retries. Setting `lockDuration` to something like 60000 (or removing the override to get the default 30s) should stop it. I started a background check on how many jobs were double-processed on staging today.

Setting `lockDuration` to something like 60000 (or removing the override to get the default 30s) should stop it. I started a background check on how many jobs were double-processed on staging today.

events.text: random q, whats the actual difference between useTransition and useDeferredValue? i always mix them up
events.text_all: random q, whats the actual difference between useTransition and useDeferredValue? i always mix them up

events.text:
```tsx
const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();
startTransition(() => setFilter(next));      // you control the update

const deferredQuery = useDeferredValue(query); // you only have the value
```

`useTransition` wraps a state update you trigger and marks it low priority, and gives you `isPending`. `useDeferredValue` is for when you receive a value (often a prop) and want a lagging copy of it, so the expensive part re-renders later while the input stays snappy. Same mechanism underneath; pick by whether you own the setter.

```python
# in the view, after form.is_valid():
if getattr(form, "gpx", None):
    hike.distance_km = round(form.gpx.length_3d() / 1000, 2)
    hike.elevation_gain_m = round(form.gpx.get_uphill_downhill().uphill)

Parse in `clean_gpx_file` so a bad file shows up as a normal form error (with a 5 MB cap), keep the parsed object on the form, and copy the numbers onto the hike in the view. events.text: random q while i wait on marco: how does postgres decide between an index scan and a bitmap heap scan
events.text_all: random q while i wait on marco: how does postgres decide between an index scan and a bitmap heap scan

events.text:
It comes down to how many rows the planner expects to match and how they're laid out on disk.

- **Index scan**: walks the index and fetches each matching row from the table right away. Great when few rows match, or when you need rows in index order (it can skip a sort). Each row fetch can be a random read, so it gets expensive as the match count grows.
- **Bitmap heap scan**: first scans the index (or several, combined with AND/OR) and builds a bitmap of which table pages contain matches, then reads those pages in physical order, once each. Better for a medium number of matches spread across many pages, because it turns random reads into mostly sequential ones. It loses the index ordering, and when the bitmap gets too big it becomes "lossy" and rechecks rows per page.
- **Seq scan** wins when a large share of the table matches.

The planner estimates selectivity from the column statistics (`pg_stats`), and weighs `random_page_cost` against `seq_page_cost` plus `effective_cache_size`. The correlation stat matters a lot: if the column is well correlated with physical order, an index scan stays cheap even for many rows. `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` shows which one it picked and how close its row estimate was.

from django.core.validators import FileExtensionValidator

def gpx_upload_to(instance, filename):
    return f"gpx/{instance.user_id}/{filename}"

class Hike(models.Model):
    ...
    gpx = models.FileField(
        upload_to=gpx_upload_to,
        blank=True,
        validators=[FileExtensionValidator(["gpx"])],
    )
```
Then `python manage.py makemigrations hikes`, add `gpx` to the hike ModelForm, and give the form `enctype="multipart/form-data"` (with htmx, add `hx-encoding="multipart/form-data"`). The extension check is only a first filter; parse the file with `gpxpy` in the form's `clean_gpx` so a renamed non-GPX file gets rejected, and cap the size there too. Set `MEDIA_ROOT`/`MEDIA_URL` locally, or use `django-storages` if you host it somewhere with S3.

```python
from django.core.validators import FileExtensionValidator

def gpx_upload_to(instance, filename):
    return f"gpx/{instance.user_id}/{filename}"

class Hike(models.Model):
    ...
    gpx = models.FileField(
        upload_to=gpx_upload_to,
        blank=True,
        validators=[FileExtensionValidator(["gpx"])],
    )
```
Then `python manage.py makemigrations hikes`, add `gpx` to the hike ModelForm, and give the form `enctype="multipart/form-data"` (with htmx, add `hx-encoding="multipart/form-data"`). The extension check is only a first filter; parse the file with `gpxpy` in the form's `clean_gpx` so a renamed non-GPX file gets rejected, and cap the size there too. Set `MEDIA_ROOT`/`MEDIA_URL` locally, or use `django-storages` if you host it somewhere with S3.

# 2026-09-16 staging ingress 404s

Status: resolved. Owner: Priya Shah.

## Timeline (UTC)
- 14:05 control plane upgraded 1.28 -> 1.29 on acme-staging
- 14:20 node groups rolled
- 14:31 staging.acme.dev returns 404 for all paths; ALB target groups empty
- 16:12 controller upgraded v2.6.2 -> v2.8.1, targets re-registered
- 16:19 recovered

## Cause
The old controller release could not reconcile Ingress objects after the
upgrade (removed API version for EndpointSlice in its client), so it stopped
registering targets. ALB stayed up with no healthy targets.

## Action items
- [x] Upgrade the controller on staging
- [ ] Add the controller step to infra/docs/runbooks/eks-upgrade.md before acme-prod

events.text: Short version: the EKS 1.29 upgrade broke the ingress. The AWS Load Balancer Controller on staging was still v2.6.2, which couldn't reconcile Ingress objects on 1.29, so it stopped registering targets and the ALB answered 404 for about 1h45m until it was upgraded to v2.8.1. The gotcha: the AWS Load Balancer Controller must be upgraded first, before the cluster goes to 1.29. The incident's open action item is still open, since `infra/docs/runbooks/eks-upgrade.md` doesn't mention the controller yet, and that matters before acme-prod gets upgraded. I'm checking which controller version prod runs in the background.

events.text: whats the actual difference between docker compose up -d and docker compose start
events.text_all: whats the actual difference between docker compose up -d and docker compose start

events.text:
- `docker compose up -d` makes reality match the compose file: it creates networks and volumes if needed, creates containers that don't exist, recreates ones whose config or image changed, then starts them detached. It's the command you want after editing `docker-compose.yml` or on a fresh machine.
- `docker compose start` only starts containers that already exist and are stopped. It never creates or recreates anything, so config changes are ignored, and it fails for services that were never created.

The pairs are `up`/`down` (create and remove) and `start`/`stop` (just run state). In practice, `up -d` is safe to use every time; `start` is only a slightly faster way to resume after a `stop`.

- `docker compose start` only starts containers that already exist and are stopped. It never creates or recreates anything, so config changes are ignored, and it fails for services that were never created.

The pairs are `up`/`down` (create and remove) and `start`/`stop` (just run state). In practice, `up -d` is safe to use every time; `start` is only a slightly faster way to resume after a `stop`.

events.text:
Two things in `billing-sync.ts` explain 30+ minute gaps, nothing changed yet:
1. It filters on `created >= lastRunAt`. Stripe invoices are created as drafts and finalized later, so an invoice created before the last run but finalized after it is skipped until it changes again, or forever.
2. `lastRunAt` is set to `new Date()` at the end of the run, not the start. Anything created while a slow run is paging through Stripe falls into the gap between the two.

The usual fix is to sync on Stripe events (`invoice.finalized`, `invoice.paid`) via `stripe.events.list` with a stored cursor, or at least record the start time and add an overlap window. Since it's billing code, I'll wait for your review before touching it. I'm not certain #1 is the cause for the specific invoices finance flagged; their invoice ids would let me check.

events.text: quick q while i get coffee: whats actually different between structuredClone(x) and JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x))
events.text_all: quick q while i get coffee: whats actually different between structuredClone(x) and JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x))

events.text:
```js
const a = { d: new Date(), m: new Map([[1, 'x']]), u: undefined };
structuredClone(a);              // Date stays a Date, Map stays a Map, u kept
JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(a));   // d becomes a string, m becomes {}, u dropped
```

structuredClone uses the same algorithm browsers use to copy data between windows and workers. It keeps Dates, Maps, Sets, typed arrays, and handles circular references. The JSON round trip only keeps plain JSON values: Dates turn into strings, Maps and Sets become empty objects, undefined and functions disappear, and a circular reference throws. Neither one copies functions or class prototypes (a class instance comes back as a plain object), and structuredClone throws on functions instead of silently dropping them.

events.text:
How it works today: on SIGTERM the worker stops taking new jobs and drains the in-flight ones, with a 30 second grace period (`GRACE_PERIOD_MS = 30_000` in services/worker/src/shutdown.ts). After 30 seconds it exits with code 1 and BullMQ marks the abandoned jobs as stalled. The Helm chart also sets `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30`, so Kubernetes would SIGKILL at the same moment anyway.

The previous pod's logs show the real problem. An image-resize job *started* about a second after SIGTERM, and the pod hit the 30s limit while it was still running. Two things are on our side: `w.close()` lets the worker pick up one more job while it's closing, and image jobs can take longer than 30s. Possible fixes are pausing the workers before close and raising both grace values together (for example 90s in the app and 100s in Helm). I haven't changed anything yet.

events.text: unrelated, trailmix question. django orm: how do i annotate each Hike with its photo count and only keep hikes with more than 3 photos
events.text_all: unrelated, trailmix question. django orm: how do i annotate each Hike with its photo count and only keep hikes with more than 3 photos

events.text:
```python
from django.db.models import Count

hikes = (
    Hike.objects
    .annotate(photo_count=Count("photos", distinct=True))
    .filter(photo_count__gt=3)
    .order_by("-photo_count")
)
```

`"photos"` is the related name of the Photo foreign key to Hike (use `photo` if you didn't set a related_name). Filtering on an annotation after `.annotate()` becomes a `HAVING` clause in SQL. Keep `distinct=True` if you also annotate across another relation like tags in the same query; otherwise the joins multiply the counts. For HTMX partials, `hike.photo_count` is then available directly in the template.

events.text: random q: Promise.all vs Promise.allSettled, when does the difference actually bite
events.text_all: random q: Promise.all vs Promise.allSettled, when does the difference actually bite

events.text:
```ts
await Promise.all([a(), b(), c()]);        // rejects as soon as one rejects
await Promise.allSettled([a(), b(), c()]); // always resolves: [{status, value|reason}, ...]
```

`Promise.all` rejects with the first error, and you lose the results of the others even though they keep running in the background. That bites when the tasks are independent, like sending ten emails: one failure throws away the information about which nine succeeded. `allSettled` waits for everything and tells you each outcome, so you can retry only the failures. Use `all` when the results only make sense together (load user + org + permissions for one page). Use `allSettled` for fan-out work where partial success is fine.

events.text: how does http/2 multiplexing actually differ from http/1.1 keep-alive? someone in standup said they're the same thing
events.text_all: how does http/2 multiplexing actually differ from http/1.1 keep-alive? someone in standup said they're the same thing

events.text: They're not the same. HTTP/1.1 keep-alive reuses one TCP connection for several requests, but one at a time: request 2 can't start until response 1 has fully arrived (pipelining existed but was broken in practice). That's why browsers open about 6 connections per host. HTTP/2 multiplexing splits every request and response into small frames tagged with a stream id and interleaves them on a single connection, so dozens of requests are in flight at once and a slow response doesn't block the others at the HTTP level. The remaining catch is TCP itself: one lost packet still stalls every stream on that connection. That head-of-line blocking is what HTTP/3 over QUIC fixes.

events.text: whats tsx actually doing differently from ts-node under the hood
events.text_all: whats tsx actually doing differently from ts-node under the hood

events.text: tsx compiles each file with esbuild and only strips the types; it doesn't type-check. That's why it starts almost instantly and handles ESM, CommonJS and tsconfig paths with no setup. ts-node uses the real TypeScript compiler by default, so it type-checks as it goes (slower to start, but it catches type errors at run time), and its ESM support needs a loader flag and has historically been fiddly. In practice: tsx for running scripts and dev servers, and keep `tsc --noEmit` in CI for the actual type checking.

events.text: is there any real perf difference between Map and a plain object for string keys
events.text_all: is there any real perf difference between Map and a plain object for string keys

events.text: Yes, for dynamic keys. A Map is built for frequent adds and deletes and doesn't degrade; objects with many changing keys fall out of V8's fast "shape" mode into slower dictionary mode, and `delete` is especially costly. For a fixed set of keys known up front (config, records), objects are as fast or faster and serialize to JSON for free. Map also keeps insertion order for all keys, has `.size`, and can't collide with prototype keys like `__proto__`.

events.text: Media queries look at the viewport: "if the screen is under 640px, do X". Container queries look at the size of a parent element: "if *this card's container* is under 400px, do X". That makes a component respond to the space it actually has, so the same chart works in a narrow sidebar on a wide screen. In Tailwind v4 you mark the parent with `@container` and use variants like `@sm:` or `@md:` on the children.

events.text:
The flicker is the `innerHTML` swap throwing away every card, including the images, which then re-decode with `loading="lazy"`. Options, in order of effort:

1. `hx-swap="innerHTML settle:0ms"` plus a CSS `.htmx-settling` rule if the flash is mostly the default settle class.
2. Add the idiomorph extension and use `hx-swap="morph:innerHTML"`; it diffs the DOM, so unchanged cards and their images stay put. Give each `<article>` a stable `id="trail-{{ trail.pk }}"` so it can match them.
3. `hx-swap="innerHTML transition:true"` to use the View Transitions API for a crossfade.

I'd go with 2; it fixes the root cause rather than hiding it.

1. `hx-swap="innerHTML settle:0ms"` plus a CSS `.htmx-settling` rule if the flash is mostly the default settle class.
2. Add the idiomorph extension and use `hx-swap="morph:innerHTML"`; it diffs the DOM, so unchanged cards and their images stay put. Give each `<article>` a stable `id="trail-{{ trail.pk }}"` so it can match them.
3. `hx-swap="innerHTML transition:true"` to use the View Transitions API for a crossfade.

I'd go with 2; it fixes the root cause rather than hiding it.

events.text: whats actually the difference between readiness and liveness, and when does startupProbe matter
events.text_all: whats actually the difference between readiness and liveness, and when does startupProbe matter

events.text:
- **Readiness**: "should this pod get traffic right now?" If it fails, the pod is removed from the Service endpoints but keeps running. Use it for warm-up and temporary overload.
- **Liveness**: "is this process stuck beyond repair?" If it fails, the kubelet restarts the container. It should only check the process itself; if it checks a database, a database blip restarts every pod at once.
- **startupProbe**: runs first and disables the other two until it succeeds. It matters when startup is slow or variable (big JIT warm-up, migrations on boot): instead of a huge `initialDelaySeconds` on liveness, you give startup a long budget (e.g. 30 x 2s) and keep liveness tight afterwards.

Rule of thumb: readiness can be strict, liveness should be dumb and lenient.

events.text:
Two separate things in that paste:

1. Job 4471 fails because `invoice.body` is null; `renderLineItems` reads `invoice.body.lines` unguarded. Likely a draft invoice with no line items yet getting emailed.
2. The OOM is a side effect: `renderInvoice` registers a `data` listener and creates a PDFDocument before the throw, and the failed docs are never ended, so their buffers pile up across retries until the heap hits ~2GB.

Fix: guard `body?.lines ?? []` and render an empty-items row, and wrap the render in try/finally that calls `doc.end()`. I'm reproducing it with a fixture invoice in the background to confirm before changing anything.

events.text:
Your view already returns just the cards for htmx requests, so put the trigger on the last card of each page:

```html
{% for trail in page %}
  <article class="trail-card"
    {% if forloop.last and page.has_next %}
      hx-get="{% url 'trails:list' %}?page={{ page.next_page_number }}"
      hx-trigger="revealed"
      hx-swap="afterend"
    {% endif %}>
    ...
  </article>
{% endfor %}
```

`revealed` fires once when the element scrolls into view, and `afterend` appends the next batch after it. If the list sits inside its own scrolling container rather than the window, use `hx-trigger="intersect once"` instead.

Add a release command to fly.toml:

```toml
[deploy]
  release_command = "python manage.py migrate --noinput"
```

Fly runs it in a temporary machine with your app's image and secrets after the build and before the new version takes traffic; if it exits non-zero, the deploy stops and the old version keeps running. Keep migrations backwards compatible with the currently running code, since there's a short window where old machines serve against the new schema.

events.text: whats the difference between `satisfies` and `as` in typescript, when do i use which
events.text_all: whats the difference between `satisfies` and `as` in typescript, when do i use which

events.text:
- `x as T` is an assertion: you tell the compiler "trust me, it's a T". It overrides inference and can hide real mistakes (`{} as User` compiles).
- `x satisfies T` is a check: the compiler verifies x is assignable to T but keeps x's own, narrower inferred type.

```ts
const routes = { home: "/", invoices: "/invoices" } satisfies Record<string, string>;
routes.invoices; // still the literal key, typo on routes.invoicez is an error

const el = document.getElementById("app") as HTMLDivElement; // you know more than TS here
```

Use `satisfies` by default for object literals and config you want validated without widening. Use `as` only when you genuinely know more than the compiler (DOM lookups, narrowing `unknown` after your own check), and prefer a type guard where you can.

Hi again,

Thanks for the quick reply on Friday. To clarify what we need, since I think my first email was vague:

Our bookkeeper (external, she uses Xero) needs a monthly file of every invoice we issued, including voided ones, with these columns in this order:

  invoice number, client name, client tax id, issue date, due date, subtotal, tax, total, currency, status, paid date

The CSV export you pointed me to on the Invoices page gives us number, client, status, total and due date only, and it only exports what is on screen (so 25 at a time), which means she has to click through pages and stitch files together.

We also have two clients billed in USD and the rest in CAD, and she needs them in separate files or at least a currency column she can filter on. She does NOT want amounts converted.

Nice to have, not essential: being able to schedule it so it lands in her inbox on the 1st of each month.

Is any of this possible today? If not, is it on the roadmap? We have been happy with Acme otherwise and would rather not move invoicing to another tool just for this.

Thanks,
Dana

# @acme/cli

Internal CLI for Acme engineers. Binary: `acme`.

## Install

```sh
npm i -g @acme/cli
```

The CLI checks for updates once a day using update-notifier. When a newer
version is on npm it prints a one-line notice to stderr after the command
finishes. Set `NO_UPDATE_NOTIFIER=1` to silence it (CI sets this already).

events.text: whats the actual difference between useTransition and useDeferredValue again, i always mix them up
events.text_all: whats the actual difference between useTransition and useDeferredValue again, i always mix them up

events.text:
```tsx
const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();
startTransition(() => setFilter(next));      // you own the state update

const deferredQuery = useDeferredValue(query); // you only receive the value
```
Both tell React that an update can wait so urgent things like typing stay responsive. The difference is where you hook in.

- `useTransition`: use it when you make the state change yourself. You wrap the setter, and you get `isPending` to show a spinner.
- `useDeferredValue`: use it when the value comes from somewhere you don't control, like a prop or a parent's state. React gives you a copy of the value that lags behind during heavy renders, and you render the slow part from that copy.

Rule of thumb: if you own the setter, use a transition. If you only have the value, defer it.

-- Paid invoice revenue per org per calendar month (UTC), last 12 months,
-- with a running total per org. Amounts stay in integer cents.
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT
    i.org_id,
    EXTRACT(YEAR FROM i.paid_at) AS yr,
    EXTRACT(MONTH FROM i.paid_at) AS mon,
    SUM(i.total_cents) AS revenue_cents,
    COUNT(*) AS invoice_count
  FROM invoices i
  WHERE i.status = 'paid'
    AND i.deleted_at IS NULL
    AND i.paid_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '1' YEAR
  GROUP BY i.org_id, EXTRACT(YEAR FROM i.paid_at), EXTRACT(MONTH FROM i.paid_at)
)
SELECT
  m.org_id,
  m.yr,
  m.mon,
  m.revenue_cents,
  m.invoice_count,
  SUM(m.revenue_cents) OVER (
    PARTITION BY m.org_id
    ORDER BY m.yr, m.mon
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
  ) AS running_revenue_cents
FROM monthly m
ORDER BY m.org_id, m.yr, m.mon;

events.text: how does AbortSignal.timeout differ from doing a manual AbortController + setTimeout? is one better
events.text_all: how does AbortSignal.timeout differ from doing a manual AbortController + setTimeout? is one better

events.text:
```ts
await fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10_000) });
```
The result is the same: the request is aborted when time runs out. The differences:

- `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` is one line, and there's no timer for you to clean up. It rejects with a `TimeoutError`, so you can tell a timeout apart from a deliberate cancel (`AbortError`).
- With a manual controller and `setTimeout`, you must `clearTimeout` once the request finishes, or the timer keeps running. It's still the right choice when you also need to cancel on other events. In that case, combine the signals with `AbortSignal.any([userSignal, AbortSignal.timeout(ms)])`.

For a plain timeout, use `AbortSignal.timeout`.

events.text: q: when k8s kills a worker pod mid deploy, what happens to the jobs that pod was in the middle of? how long do they get before its yanked
events.text_all: q: when k8s kills a worker pod mid deploy, what happens to the jobs that pod was in the middle of? how long do they get before its yanked

events.text: I don't know for sure how our worker handles it, and I'd rather not guess. In general, Kubernetes sends the pod a stop signal, waits for the pod's configured termination timeout, and then force-kills it. What happens to in-flight jobs depends on whether the worker catches that signal and lets running jobs finish before it exits. If it doesn't, the jobs are interrupted, and the queue picks them up again later because their lock expires. To answer for our setup, I'd need to look at the worker's shutdown code and the termination setting in its Helm chart. Want me to check both?

In general, Kubernetes sends the pod a stop signal, waits for the pod's configured termination timeout, and then force-kills it. What happens to in-flight jobs depends on whether the worker catches that signal and lets running jobs finish before it exits. If it doesn't, the jobs are interrupted, and the queue picks them up again later because their lock expires. # @acme/cli

Internal command-line tool for Acme.

## Install

```sh
npm install -g @acme/cli
```

## Usage

### acme invoices list

List invoices for the current org.

```sh
acme invoices list [--status <status>] [--limit <n>] [--json]
```

| Option | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `--status` | all | Filter by draft, sent, paid, overdue or void |
| `--limit` | 25 | Max rows (1-100) |
| `--json` | false | Print JSON instead of a table |

## License

MIT
